analysis.evidence: The land (הָאָרֶץ) is the subject and אֹתָם (“them”) is the object. The clause כִּי הָיָה רְכוּשָׁם רָב explains why the land could not support Abram and Lot together: their possessions were too great.
analysis.morphology: Qal perfect, third-person masculine singular, with no prefix or suffix. The verb precedes its feminine singular subject הָאָרֶץ.

analysis.evidence: וְלֹא נָשָׂא אֹתָם הָאָרֶץ says that the land could not support them. The reason given, כִּי הָיָה רְכוּשָׁם רָב, identifies the land as the territory where they were trying to live together with their many possessions.
analysis.morphology: The definite article הָ precedes a common noun of both genders in the singular absolute state. The noun is the subject of נָשָׂא.

analysis.evidence: יַחְדָּו supplies “together.” The land could not support both households because their possessions were so great, so לָשֶׁבֶת refers to living in the same place.
analysis.morphology: The prefixed preposition לָ introduces the Qal infinitive construct שֶׁבֶת.
analysis.sense: to dwell habitually in a place

analysis.evidence: In לָשֶׁבֶת יַחְדָּו, the adverb modifies לָשֶׁבֶת, “to dwell.” The land could not support Abram and Lot living in the same place because their possessions were so extensive.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew adverb with no separate prefix or pronominal suffix.

analysis.evidence: כִּי introduces הָיָה רְכוּשָׁם רָב, “their possessions were great,” giving the reason the land could not support them living together.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew conjunction with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: In כִּי הָיָה רְכוּשָׁם רָב, “because their property was abundant,” הָיָה links the subject רְכוּשָׁם to the adjective רָב. The abundance of their property explains why they could not live together.
analysis.morphology: Qal perfect, third person masculine singular, agreeing with רְכוּשָׁם, “their property.”
analysis.sense: to be in a state or condition
